title: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpon Thursday said that ifTexasSenate nomineeKen Paxtonloses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen.John Cornynand conservative commentatorKarl Rove.

Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed.

"If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle.Most recent pollsshow state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.

The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nomineeKamala Harrisby nearly 14 percentage points.

Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.

Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.

Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.

GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.

Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Socialpost.

In a Wall Street Journalop-edtwo days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
content:
CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followedWednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure.Nebiusalso sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and andIrenultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares ofMicron TechnologyandAdvanced Micro Devicessold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memoobtainedby CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts includingMicrosoft,Meta,IBMandCaterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening.Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
content:
DemocraticTexasSenate candidateJames Talaricoraised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record asRepublicanspour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nomineeKen Paxtonin the2026 midterm election.

The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set bySouth CarolinaDemocrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.

Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.

“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.

The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.

The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with theFEC.The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.

But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.

SpaceXandTeslaCEOElon Muskhas emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC, while hisAmerica PAChas spent about $9.4 millionattackingTalarico and another $1.8 millionsupportingPaxton, according to FEC filings.

The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.

No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988.But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% inFiftyPlusOne's polling average, a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.

Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in thethird quarter of 2018during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
content:
The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.

Thelawsuitis the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which PresidentDonald Trumphas often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.

The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."

The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.

Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality."

"Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.

The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in aletterto California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.

The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County.

McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one.

"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.

Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls."

"Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing."

"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."

Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."

She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."

"My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.

CNBC has requested comment from Weber's office about the lawsuit.

title: Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
content:
Tim CookandMark Zuckerberghave clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins atApple, the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.

Metaand Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily runMeta'snew open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.

The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-calledmixture-of-experts architecture. As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.

Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.

Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Metaestimatedin early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.

Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Opencollaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.

Zuckerbergposteda picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."

Ternusresponded, "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerfulopen-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.

The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market thatNvidiahas dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.

"We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips andpublished technical documentationabout its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.

Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.

Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.

Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.

The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which hasbecome a point of contentionin Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its olderopen-weight Llama family of models, it has since focused on creating proprietary models under theleadership of Wang, who joined Meta when the companyinvested more than $14 billioninto his former startup Scale AI last year.

While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.

"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEONat Friedman, was a major Zuckerberghirelast year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.

Their leaders have also traded harsh words.

Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.

Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.

Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.

And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.

Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.

In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration "dramatically underperformed" and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute withElon Musk's xAI.ApplesuedOpenAIin July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal withGoogle, to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.

Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.

Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Musepersonal agent appand itslatest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder,released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.

Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbedMuse Glimmer, with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.

Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.

"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
content: Image source,Sirachai Arunrugstichai/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBySimon JackBusiness editorPublished1 hour agoSenior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.The biggest four banks collectively made around Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".What is the Budget and what could be in it?The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.The sector contributed nearly Â£40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.The bank levy generated Â£1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further Â£1.2bn.There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around Â£2bn a year.The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra Â£1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.Get in touchDo you have comments or questions about this story? Get in touch.Contact formRelated topicsUK economyJohn HealeyBankingUK bankingTaxMore on this storyBurnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladderPublished27 SeptemberHealey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of BudgetPublished5 hours agoFaisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the BudgetPublished1 day ago

title: Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done
content:
Wall Street estimates for the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation indicator now expect an acceleration from the level that prompted the central bank to hike rates last month.

The estimates come after ahotter-than-expected producer price indexcame in at 1.3% Thursday, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and more than double the 0.6% consensus.

That drove the year-over-year increase to 6.3%, the biggest jump since December 2022. The increase was paced by a 20% rise in gasoline prices. But taking out food, energy and trade services, prices still rose a healthy 0.5%, indicating that inflation was broader than just energy.

Seven Wall Street estimates gathered by CNBC show core personal consumption expenditures inflation for September, which will be published later this month, is forecast to rise 0.32%, up from 0.25% in August. Wall Street economists use theconsumer price index, released Wednesday, and the PPI to estimate the PCE.

"We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time even as recent Fedspeak tempered expectations for back-to-back increases,'' wrote Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.

Several Fed officials have argued that the Fed does not need to hurry to hike rates, though they have suggested more rate hikes are needed. As a result, Fed futures on Thursday showed just a 29% probability of a hike at the Fed meeting at the end of this month, but a 91% probability of at least one hike by December.

A 0.32% increase in PCE would boost the year-over-year core inflation rate to 3.1%, up from 3.01% in August. Estimates ranged from a high of 0.35% from Barclays to a low of 0.29% from Oxford Economics.

"The picture is not benign with inflation elevated and intensifying," wrote Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities. "On the economic data alone, there is little reason for the Fed to hesitate to continue moving the policy rate higher."

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has suggested one litmus test for not hiking is confidence that inflation will return in a timely manner to the Fed's 2% target. Both headline and core PCE inflation have been above target since 2021. They have inched steadily higher since tariffs were introduced in April 2025. The gains have accelerated since the beginning of the Iran war.

The Fed prefers the PCE because, compared to the CPI, it believes it more closely resembles how Americans actually spend their money and changes its weightings when consumers change their spending patterns.

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByArchie MitchellBusiness reporterPublished15 October 2026, 14:07 BSTUpdated 1 minute agoCulture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed Â£1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal."We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".The two companies announced in Julythat Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite showsPublished6 JulyBut Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:The need for free expression of opinion in news mediaThe need for a range of views in news media across the UKThe need for a range of people controlling the media across the UKThe need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UKThe letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.A Sky spokesperson said: "We havealready made clear commitmentsto protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process."This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."Related topicsDepartment for Digital, Culture, Media & SportSkyITV

title: U.S. reportedly considers use of 'mother of all bombs' as Iran vows to fight on
content:
The U.S. military has drawn up options for renewed strikes on Iran that include the potential use of one of the biggest nonnuclear bombs in its arsenal,CNN reported Thursday, as Tehran vowed to continue fighting for its demands.

The strike plans involve the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, nicknamed the "mother of all bombs," CNN reported, citing multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter.

CNBC has not independently confirmed the report. An official told CNBC the Defense Department "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."

The 21,600-pound airburst weapon is designed to affect surface targets over a wide area and has so far not been deployed by the U.S. in previous strikes on targets inside Iran. It wasused in Afghanistan in 2017during the previous Trump administration.

U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpsaid last weekthat he would not order a resumption of military strikes before themidterm electionson Nov. 3.

Tensions in the Middle East are nonetheless elevated amid thesinking of a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesdayand a string offatal attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The White House is undermounting pressureto show progress in its Middle East objectives ahead of the midterms, as the American public increasingly feels the impact at home viasoaring energy pricesandwider cost pressures.

Tehran isreportedly strengthening its defensesaround sensitive energy and nuclear sites in preparation for a potential resumption of attacks, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a televised address late Wednesday that Iran must continue to use a combination of military and defensive capabilities, negotiations, and regional strategic leverage to push the U.S. to accept its demands.

Officials in Tehran have previously listed demandsincludingWashington lifting its naval blockade and sanctions and withdrawing U.S. military forces from the region.

Ghalibaf said Tehran's goal is not to be locked in an endless war, but to prevent the U.S. and its other adversaries from being able to achieve their own objectives through military attacks, Iranian state-affiliated media reported.

title: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
content:
September'sproducer price indexcame in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energy amid the U.S. war with Iran.

The measure of underlying inflation pressures climbed 1.3% in September and 6.3% on an annual basis, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That marked the largest monthly and annual gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively.

Both readings topped expectations of economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast an advance of 0.6% on the month and 5.5% annually.

Energy drove a sizable chunk of those increases as the Middle East conflict curtailed oil supply and sent prices surging. The so-called core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices from the wholesaler inflation index, added 0.7% on the month and 5% over the 12-month period.

But there are signs that soaring energy prices are having downstream effects on other categories. The BLS said in Thursday's release that almost half of September's increase in processed goods for immediate demand was connected to the rise in diesel fuel prices.

It's the latest report in recent days showing that inflation continues to hit consumers and companies.

Wednesday'sconsumer price indexrelease showed a rise of 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% on a 12-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.

Excluding food and energy, the core CPI added 0.3% on the month and 2.6% compared with a year ago. Economists anticipated increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.

Wednesday's Beige Book, a chronicle of economic activity published by theFederal Reserve, had the highest number of mentions of terms related to inflation on record, according to an analysis from Bespoke Investment Group.

Retail sales grew 0.8% in September, surpassing the rate of 0.4% anticipated by economists, according to government data released in a separate report Thursday. That marked a slowdown from a month prior, when retail sales rose by more than 1%.

Excluding spending on autos and gas stations, retail sales increased 0.25% from August to September, a drop from around 1.1% in the prior period. This slowdown offers a sign that high prices related to fuel are causing consumers to tighten the belt elsewhere.

This week's data has left a growing minority of fed funds futures traders expecting the central bank to raise rates at its meeting later this month. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 34% likelihood that the Fed hikes borrowing costs on Oct. 28, up from under 18% a week prior, according to CME's FedWatch tool. About 90% expect at least one hike by the end of the year.

"With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, investing chief at Northlight Asset Management.

These reports offer some of the final insights into the pace of inflation in the U.S. ahead of themidterm election, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.

title: Southwest is overhauling its frequent flyer program. Here's what's changing
content:
Goodbye, A-List and A-List Preferred.

Southwest Airlinesis scrapping its two-tier loyalty program starting next year and instead rolling out silver, gold and platinum levels that are similar to what other carriers offer, as the once-quirky airline seeks to increase revenue and reward its biggest spenders.

Southwest executives have been overhauling the airline, getting rid of longtime customer perks like two free checked bags andopen seating. It's nowchargingfor some of those options, likerivalshave been doing for years.

Along with the shift from two to three loyalty levels, the carrier is also changing the names of its tiers. Under the old version, travelers could be classified into A-List or A-List Preferred, which was the higher level.

"If you think about A-List and A-List Preferred, we don't even have [boarding] groups A, B and C anymore," Tony Roach, Southwest chief customer and brand officer, said in an interview. "So it was time to do a refresh to somewhat incorporate all the changes to seating and all these new experiences that we've been adding."

Here's what's changing for the loyalty program:

Customers can earn 1 Tier Qualifying Point, or TQP, per $1 spent on Southwest co-branded credit cards withChase. Here are the new status requirements:

Silver status members will board in Group 1, while Gold members will board before Group 1. Platinum members will board before both Gold members and Group 1. Platinum tier also has unlimited Companion Pass trips.

Southwest's Companion Pass — which lets a designated person fly for free, minus taxes and fees, with a traveler who has that perk — is also changing.

Companion Pass holders that have them in their accounts will be able to hold onto them for the duration of their term. But starting with the 2027 earning year, Companion Pass benefits will be earned through TQPs or qualifying flights, by hitting a milestone reward or with Platinum status.

Currently, a Rapid Rewards member has to earn at least 135,000 qualifying points or 100 one-way flights to qualify for the pass.

The airline is also expanding its partnerships with international airlines and building its first airport lounges. Southwest on Thursday offered a peek into thenew lounges, which it has named Icon, and is working on with its credit card partner,Chase. The carrier is building Icon lounges in four cities around the U.S., with others in the works.

Southwest is also adding benefits for customers that are in between status tiers, similar to whatAmerican Airlinesoffers.

For example, after earning 20,000 points or taking 15 qualifying flights, customers can choose between 2,000 more Rapid Rewards points or two coupons to select a "preferred" seat, which is a standard legroom seat that's closer to the front of the plane or a more popular aisle or window seat.

Customers will also get three Companion Pass trips after earning 95,000 points or taking 75 qualifying flights, which is below the Platinum threshold.

"That is definitely different from what we've done before," said Nandika Suri, who heads Southwest's Rapid Rewards loyalty program. She said the new strategy is "a way for us to actually recognize and reward customers ... faster and more frequently in their journey to continue to engage with us."

Airlines overall have consistently raised the requirements to earn status, requiring more spending, and have made similarchangesto enter their airport lounges.

United Airlineson Tuesday said it would no longer allow customers to earn status in its Mileage Plus program based on flight segments next year and that it would only accept Premier qualifying points, which are earned from flight spending and on a co-branded credit card.

United also raised the requirements to reach Premier 1K, its highest frequent flyer tier outside of the invite-only Global Services, to 32,000 qualifying points, up from 28,000 this year.

— CNBC'sCaleigh Keatingcontributed to this article.

title: Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations
content:
Amazonon Thursdayunveiledtwo new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.

The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor.

Amazon acquiredBee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.

The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.

Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.

The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said.

Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of newAI hardware. Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infusedAlexa Tablets, whileMicrosoftshowcased anNvidia-powered Windows laptop andAppleunveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.

The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market.

Metahas seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers.

Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant calledMuse Charmthat runs its latest Muse AI assistant.Plauddeveloped a card-shaped note-taking device, andFriendoffers an AI necklace.

Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.

When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions.

With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.

The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said.

An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.

title: U.S. Treasury dismisses IMF debt warning and 'messy' forecasting
content:
The International Monetary Fund should check its own forecasting record before criticizing U.S. fiscal policy, David Zervos,newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary, said on Thursday.

"When we see pieces on the IMF, it's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," Zervos said in emailed comments to CNBC.

The former Wall Street economist was responding to the IMF's Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, who cautioned during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday that strong U.S. economic growth wouldnot be sufficient to put mounting federal debton a sustainable course.

Georgieva was herself responding to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in August that the U.S. could"grow our way out"of a rising debt-to-GDP ratio, aftergovernment debt surpassed $40 trillion.

Zervos, formerly chief market strategist at Jefferies, said Thursday: "In 2008, [the IMF's World Economic Outlook] hadworld growth at 3%and we had the first global contraction in post-world history a year later. We saw them positive on Southeast Asia in 1997 before the collapse."

"We saw them very negative on Russia in 2022, and Russia actually barely saw a blip down in growthbefore it started growing strongly. We saw them very positive on Argentina after theirbig bailout of $57 billion. And by 2020,Argentina was basically in default again. And the history books go on and on, whether it's Greece, whether it was thetransitory call on inflationin the U.S."

"So take it all with a grain of salt," he added.

Many economists warn thatmounting U.S. interest paymentsand ahigh deficithave raised the risk of an unsustainable debt spiral. However, they are divided on whether the U.S. could be pushed into atrue fiscal crisis.

The IMF's Georgieva has issued similar warnings to other big economies over the need for fiscal consolidation, telling CNBC on Oct. 7 that hermessage to France was: "Get your house in order."

Other economic institutions are also sounding the alarm over the rising cost of servicing global debt, whichtopped $365 trillion in the first half of the year. The Institute of International Finance argued in a September report that a "vicious cycle between elections and short-term quick fixes" to debt challenges was reducing the ability to spend money on public services.

title: What to know about Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused Starlink service
content:
Uncertainty over who controls SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention, as restrictions on the technology hinder Ukraine's defenses.

Ukraine has accusedSpaceX-owned Starlink ofrestricting its military-grade services, known as Starshield, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv.

Officials in Kyiv said SpaceX had imposed restrictions on Starshield without advance notice, disrupting military operations and hampering efforts to protect civilians amid intense Russian attacks this week.

In response, SpaceX CEOElon Muskappeared to shift responsibility for any changes to Starshield's use in Ukraine to the U.S. government and PresidentDonald Trump. He said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by Washington, with the U.S. military and ultimately the president determining any limits on their use. The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately reply to CNBC's request for comment.

Here's what to know about Starshield, and how it differs from Starlink.

Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology and launch capabilities of its Starlink service.

According to SpaceX, Starshield currently focuses on Earth observation, secure global communications for government users, and so-called "hosted payloads," which refers to hosting specialized equipment aboard satellites for customers.

Unlike Starlink, which serves consumers and businesses, Starshield offers enhanced security features, including high-assurance cryptographic capability designed to handle classified information. It says its satellites can handle a range of equipment and connect with other satellites through laser communications technology.

SpaceX was awarded over $6 billion in multi-year U.S. government contracts for Starshield, primarily from two major Space Force contracts for low Earth orbit-based communications and sensing constellations, SpaceX said in itslatest earnings report.

Musk on Wednesdaydistinguished Starshieldfrom SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, which he said was restricted to civilian and defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations.

Although Starshield serves a different purpose from Starlink's commercial internet service, which provides high-speed connectivity to regular people, the two are closely connected.

Starlink is SpaceX's general satellite internet service, sold for consumer, civilian, and defense purposes, and offers internet access in remote areas where it has traditionally been limited.

Starshield uses stronger encryption and specialized terminals for secure communications, but relies on Starlink's extensive satellite network to operate.

According to SpaceX, Starlink operates in more than 160 countries, territories and other markets, offering residential plans starting at $55 per month. The company says its service can deliver download speeds exceeding 400 megabits per second in most locations.

title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
content:
Long-termbond yieldsabove 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory.

Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future.

The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average30-year fixed rate mortgagehovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales dropped 4% in September,Redfinsaid Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

Mortgage ratestrack the10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed climbed 123 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through Wednesday's close, when the 10-year traded at 5.19%.

Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war in Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.

In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and thecompetition for capital among them is intensifyingas companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market.

If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields.

But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought totarget a deficitlower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term.

There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The Treasury Department will in the next few days give official results for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September. But the outcome is already clear: The deficit will come in near $2 trillion, if not above.

That is likely to put the deficit in the range of 6.0-6.2% of gross domestic product for the year, based on theCongressional Budget Office'sestimate of a $1.993 trillion deficit and a projection of third quarter GDP.

Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher,the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits.

CBOexpects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared to 5.3% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years.

"My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.

AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to theCommittee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets.

GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy.

Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.

In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker,wants to reversethe $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package.

And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties.

The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much farther out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.

For now, though higher yields are alsoattracting investorsto U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips.

Here are TSMC's third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

The world's largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier.

TSMC's third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors.

TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company's earnings call.

The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand.

TSMC's stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company's elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email.

TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process.

Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC's careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems.

"Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity," he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers' ability to deploy the chips they order.

Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC's total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips.

By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate.

TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors.

The company's free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago.

TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain.

TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule.

TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earningsannouncementin July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona.

The chipmaker is alsoreportedlyconsidering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.

title: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, shattering hopes of an 'energy ceasefire'
content:
PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyhas said Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Moscow failed to uphold its end of an "energy ceasefire"dealproposed by PresidentDonald Trump.

"The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done,"Zelenskyy told the Financial Timesafter Ukraine paused strikes on energy targets for three days at the request of Washington.

On Sunday, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia in an effort to put an end to the countries attacking each other's power facilities and thereby lower the price of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month.

Despite Ukraine's pause, officials in Kyiv said the country has been stripped of advance warnings of incoming ballistic missiles, as Starlink connectivity services had been restricted across the country, disrupting military operations. The restrictions apply to the sister service Starshield.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday thatSpaceXhasimplemented a speed limiton Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces.

"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram.

According to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, the U.S. government isultimately responsible for any curbson Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X on Wednesday.

The White House and SpaceX didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment.

In an interview with Piers Morgan released late Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he felt let down by Trump's recent dealings with Vladimir Putin, Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the apparent shutdown of Starlink.

Asked whether he felt "betrayed by what has been happening," Zelenskyy answered: "Really, yes," but stressed that Ukraine's survival and its strategic relationship with the U.S. mattered more than his personal emotions.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine had honored a proposed energy ceasefire for three days, refraining from both attacks and retaliation, while Russia subsequently launched a massive assault on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles.

He said he had warned U.S. officials that Russia would violate the ceasefire and described the reported Starlink shutdown as an "absolutely crazy" move that was not consistent with the behavior expected between partners.

title: India’s IDBI Bank falls 7% as government announces $5.5 billion stake sale to Canada's Fairfax
content:
Shares ofIDBI Bankfell more than 7% Thursday after the Indian government announced a majority stake sale in the state-owned bank to Canadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings for over 529 billion rupees ($5.5 billion).

Once the final approvals are in place, the dealwill mark the largest foreign direct investmenttransaction in India's financial sector, India's Ministry of Finance said in a release on Wednesday.

"Due to its poor financial health, the [IDBI] Bank required repeated infusion of capital," the ministry said, adding that after a brief recovery, the government decided to sell a 60.7% stake in the bank to a "Strategic Buyer."

During the bidding process, the government arrived at an average fair value of IDBI shares at 75.99 rupees apiece. Fairfax's winning bid offered a price of 81 rupees per share, as per the government release.

Shares of IDBI had closed at 90.39 rupees on Wednesday, higher than Fairfax's winning bid. Fairfax will need to present credentials to the Indian banking regulator, the Reserve Bank of India, for a "fit and proper assessment."

"Having supported the bank's recovery, we arenow enabling its next phaseof growth through the infusion of Foreign Direct Investment while retaining a minority stake," India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said in a post on X Wednesday.

She added that Fairfax's investment reinforced that "India's growth story is strong, its economy is resilient, and the government's commitment to reform is unwavering."

TheIndian government has sold sharesin several companies, includingCochin Shipyard,Indian Railways Finance Corp,NHPC, andCoal India, earlier this year. In August, it raked in $3.3 billion by selling a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer,Life Insurance Corporation of India.

The government has beendivesting its stake in severalstate-owned companies this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures.

title: 'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
content: Image caption,Apurv Patel said he paid Synetal Solutions Â£3,600 and claimed he was verbally promised a guaranteed sponsored jobByMeghan OwenLondon work and money correspondentPublished5 hours agoA company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket.Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors.But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for.London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the governmentstopped overseas recruitment for care workers,external. The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical".Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious".'Miserable'Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions Â£3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs.Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said."I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said."It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances."Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless".Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work."She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said.The company disputes claims that training was ineffective.He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days.Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice.The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for Â£5,500.Home Office guidance,externalstates agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment.Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances."As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform.The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees.The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary.Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco.The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles.The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked.Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training.Image caption,Daniel Blake says the way Synetal Solutions has operated is unethicalDaniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative"."The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status."This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility."For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business."He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice."If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said.The company's website states: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed."Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK.Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid Â£3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas.Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring.To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan.Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training."The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said.The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company.Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa".It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme.The couple said Synetal Solutions had since stopped responding to their messages."We're desperate," Sarah said. "We don't see any other way out."Image caption,Amisha - not her real name - says her certificates were rejected as invalid by one company she had an interview withAmisha, whose name has also been changed, said she signed up with Synetal after being told that both a placement and visa sponsorship were guaranteed.Her student visa is due to expire soon.She said the training consisted of three sessions lasting around 90 minutes each.After paying an initial instalment of Â£1,800, she became reluctant to make a second payment because she felt she had received little in return. She said the company warned her that her contract would be cancelled if she failed to pay, prompting her to transfer a further Â£1,800."I was waiting for interviews for two or three months. They were ignoring me," she said.According to Amisha, the company applied for only a handful of vacancies advertised on job-search website Indeed. She eventually secured an interview for a healthcare assistant role, but said the employer told her the certificates she had received were not recognised.Image source,Unknown CopyrightImage caption,A screenshot of a supposed testimonial from Synetal Solutions' website with content that does not appear to make senseThe BBC also identified what appeared to be at least a couple of stock photographs or AI-generated images used as testimonials on the company's website.The company said it had not authenticated the two reviews identified, and removed them after we contacted them.Image source,OTS SolicitorsImage caption,Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said the promises being made to individuals facing visa deadlines were "particularly concerning"Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said it was "particularly concerning" where individuals facing visa deadlines were being asked to make substantial payments on the understanding that jobs, sponsorship or immigration outcomes were seemingly guaranteed.She urged caution, adding that a job offer alone does not guarantee someone will be able to remain in the UK."The outcome can depend on the role, the sponsor, the individual meeting the relevant immigration requirements and, ultimately, any decision by the Home Office," she said.'Go to the police'Blake told the BBC: "If it seems good to be true, it probably is. If you are considering handing over money upfront then seek advice."He said that "if people have given money and haven't received the service that they were entitled to they should seek redress"."First of all, make a complaint directly to the company, then to Trading Standards."If people feel a criminal offence has happened, we would encourage and support them to go to the police."A government spokesperson said: "We know how much distress scammers cause to their victims, which is why we will do everything in our power to protect hardworking families and vulnerable customers."Our reforms have provided Companies House with new and improved powers to prevent companies from acting unlawfully and to query, remove and share suspicious information."Synetal Solutions said: "We provide training and employment assistance and maintain supporting records. Recruitment, sponsorship and visa decisions depend on employers and the Home Office."The company said it had records of genuine candidates who had secured jobs and sponsorship through its services.Get in touchHave you been affected by issues covered in this story?
