title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
content: Image source,Getty Images for HubSpotImage caption,Anthropic chief executive Dario AmodeiByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished15 October 2026, 02:14 BSTUpdated 1 hour agoArtificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (Â£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have fallen in recent days over concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure.An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. Trading on South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq was temporarily halted after falling by more than 8%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by over 5%.How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm electionsPublished6 hours ago'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfirePublished20 hours agoThe falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".There also been concerns over the safety of AI models.OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodeicalling on the pace of development to slow down.The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday.Related topicsInternational BusinessArtificial intelligence

title: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems
content:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.

Writing on X,Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."

Ukraine had accusedSpaceXof imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.

On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyon defense technology, saidSpaceXhad implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.

That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he saidon Telegram. Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.

Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.

Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorovthanking Muskearly Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.

The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an"energy ceasefire,"between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians ofbreaching the ceasefire.

Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.

Washington hasthreatenedto cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.

— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

title: Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO
content:
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion as it prepares for a highly anticipated initial public offering reportedly slated for November, according to people familiar with the matter.

Revenue rose from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, with first-quarter revenue at $4.7 billion, the people said, adding that Anthropic said it was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter.

The company also told investors it was cash-flow positive, generating $1.70 in revenue for every dollar spent on computing power during the third quarter, according to the Financial Times. Investors expect Anthropic to reach $110 billion in annualized revenue by year-end, according to The Wall Street Journal.

CNBC previouslyreportedthat the Claude maker planned to disclose its third-quarter financial results for the first time at a meeting with potential investors, including institutional investors, citing two people familiar with the matter.

title: Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms to raise up to $3.2 billion in historic IPO in India
content:
Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms, India's largest telecom operator, is looking to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through aninitial public offeringof shares.

Jio Platforms will sell 270 million shares inIPO pricedbetween 1,065 rupees and 1,119 rupees apiece, from Oct. 21 to Oct. 23. Reliance Industries, the parent company of the telecom operator, said in an exchange filing.

The share sale will be India's largest ever in rupee terms, but the second largest in dollar terms, marginally trailing the Hyundai Motors IPO thatraised $3.3 billionin 2024. As per estimates provided by Indian market intelligence firm Prime Database, Jio was expected to raise around 377 billion rupees through its IPO.

At the top end of the price range, Jio Platforms is valued at around $108 billion, muchlower than previously expected. While Jio Platforms has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider, investors seem unconvinced.

Jio Platforms, at its core, is a telecom company, Deven Choksey, managing director of Mumbai-based DRChoksey Finserv, told CNBC.

While entertainment or gaming applications owned by Jio Platforms increase data consumption, the company earns revenues primarily from selling internet data, he added.

Jio is the largest telecom company in India with over half a million subscribers, but at its current price it will be valued less than Bharti Airtel, the second largest player in the country. Bharti Airtel has a market cap of $117.5 billion, as per LSEG data.

Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's flagship company,Reliance Industries, ownsmore than a 66% stakein Jio Platforms, followed byMeta Platforms' affiliate Jaadhu Holdings that owns nearly 10% andGoogleInternational, which owns 7.7%, as per LSEG data.

Neither Meta nor Google will sell their stake in the company, according to the IPO papers.

Jio Platforms also plans to roll out satellite communications services in India, putting it at thecenter of the spatbetween owner Ambani and Starlink's Elon Musk. Jio is reportedly looking to set up a network of around 1,600 LEO satellites and 23 ground stations to expand connectivity across India.

Musk, last Saturday, accused Ambani ofblocking Starlink's launchin India to maintain his "monopolistic exploitation" of the Indian market.

title: SK Hynix plunges 8% amid Asia tech rout as Fed rate hike fears, AI funding worries mount
content:
A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday, with Asian chipmakers tracking Wall Street losses as concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, financing of artificial intelligence investments weigh on sentiment.

South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 7.1%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.1%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 7.7% and Samsung SDI declined 6.8%.

In Japan, technology investment giantSoftBank Grouptumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment makerAdvantestdropped 6.9%, while chipmaking equipment supplierTokyo Electronlost 5.4%.Renesas Electronicsdeclined 5.4%.

The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.

The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.

title: Inside India newsletter: Billionaire Ambani’s mega-IPO faces a valuation reality check amid Musk spat
content:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of"Inside India"— your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

Indian tycoon Mukesh Ambani, whose plans to launch satellite communications and dominance over the Indian telecom market have drawn the ire of Elon Musk last week, has a more pressing worry.

Jio Platforms, the company at the center of Musk's remarks, is coming up with a record IPO issue soon, but its valuation demands have met with pushback from investors who seem unconvinced of the company's positioning as a tech business.

Any thoughts on today's newsletter?Share themwith the team.

Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's telecom and digital services business Jio Platforms, which was called "monopolistic" by Starlink founder Elon Musk last week, has lowered its valuation ahead of its initial public offering next week.

Jio Platforms is the largest telecom operator in India with over half a million subscribers but has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider, experts told CNBC, but disagreed on whether these demands were valid.

Jio Platforms' IPO will raise up to 302 billion rupees (nearly $3.2 billion) at a price band of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees per share, its parent companyReliance Industriessaid in a stock filing on Wednesday. This values the company at around $108 billion—lower than the valuations of over $130 billion floated a year ago.

Jio's enterprise valuation has shrunk to $118 billion from the $133 billion expected earlier, global brokerage Nomura said in a report on Sunday based onBloomberg newslast week that revealed the IPO pricing details.

Reliance Industries, the parent company of Jio Platforms, did not respond to CNBC's emails seeking comments.

An equity valuation of $108 billion places Jio lower than India's second-largest telecom company Bharti Airtel, which currently trades at a market capitalization of over $117 billion, as per LSEG data.

"Following its listing, Jio will likely need to demonstrate growth to public shareholders," the report said, adding that the era of "easy subscriber gains" is ending and tariff hikes are likely to become "the primary driver of earnings growth."

As per the information shared in Jio Platforms' IPO papers, the company's ARPU was 214 rupees ($2.25) per month while that of its competitor Airtel was 257 rupees for mobile, 527 rupees for home internet and 158 rupees for digital TV services.

Based purely on average revenue per user, a key metric for telecom companies, Jio's discount to Airtel seems justified, but Jio wants to be seen as a tech company and not just a utility player.

Through the IPO, Jio Platforms plans to clear off its legacy telecom debt, which will free up internal cash flows for its second phase of growth, according to Neil Shah, a partner at Counterpoint Research.

Jio plans to use the funds raised by the IPO to pay off its telecom business debt of 275 billion rupees, according to its IPO papers.

The next phase of investment will involve funding the company's "gigawatt-scale green AI infrastructure" and low-earth-orbit satellite network, Shah said, placing it in the realm of tech businesses.

He pointed out that global tech majors likeMetaandGoogle, which holdnearly 10% and 8% stakesrespectively in Jio, are not exiting their investments via the IPO—proving their willingness to wait for the next phase of growth.

During the company's annual shareholder meeting in June, Ambani told shareholders that Jio will "demonstrate to the world that India canbuild technology companiesof global scale, global capability, and global value."

He highlighted that, as per the World Intellectual Property Organization, Jio Platforms' ranking in terms of "velocity of innovation through patents" jumped to 20 from 340 a year ago.

This was also when Ambani announced Jio Platforms' plan to enter the satellite communication space in India, an area that has drawn interest from Musk's Starlink. Last week, Musk said that his company has spent "five years complyingwith every single law and requirement" of the government andblamed Ambanifor the delays in the launch of Starlink.

But even as the world's first trillionaire and India's second-richest businessman contest to provide internet to the remote areas of India, some experts are not convinced Jio Platforms has enough to be defined as a tech company.

Jio Platforms wants tech prices, but they have "no product expertise" as of now, Anurag Singh, managing partner and founder of U.S. based Ansid Capital, told CNBC.

He added that while Indian investors may buy Jio's tech pitch due to lack of choice, "global investors won't." For now, Reliance is a utility company and will need significant investment to transform into a tech player, Singh said.

As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as 'mother of democracy'Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a "mother of democracy," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying.

India calls JD Vance's comments about immigrants 'deeply offensive'India on Friday called comments by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance aboutimmigrants from the country"deeply offensive". A day earlier, Vance said thatforeign and local companies"cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."

India's retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimatesIndia's headlineinflation rose to 5.54%in September from4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy. The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%

The Indian billionaire investing in Trump's refinery project is also buying more Venezuelan crudeIndian billionaire Mukesh Ambani'sReliance Industries, which is investing in a historic U.S. oil refinery project proposed by President Donald Trump, has nowemerged as the biggest buyerof Venezuelan crude outside the U.S.

title: S&P 500 futures fall as traders await more U.S. economic data: Live updates
content:
Futures tied to the S&P 500 slid on Wednesday night, with traders looking ahead to more earnings reports and economic data following a losing session brought about by hotter-than-expected inflation data.

S&P 500 futuresslipped 0.2%, whileNasdaq-100 futuresdropped 0.7%.Dow Jones Industrial Average futuresrose just 22 points.

The tech-heavyNasdaq Compositeshed 1.9% during regular trading, marking its worst day since July 23 — when it dropped 2.2%. TheS&P 500dropped 1.1%, its biggest one one-day slide since July 29. TheDowwas the relative outperformer, falling just 0.1%.

In Asia, futures for Hong Kong'sHang Seng indexstood at 24,074 lower than the index's last close of 24,314.17. Japan'sNikkei 225was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago futures at 66,225, compared with the index's previous close of 67,744.29. Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was down 0.85% in its first hour of trade.

There are growing concerns that theFederal Reservecould tighten monetary policy more aggressively before year-end, after new data showedconsumer pricesin September rose faster than expected on a year-over-year basis.

"Inflation is cooking with gas," said Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group. "It is abundantly clear where the inflation impulse originates, but two wars need to end before we get any relief. The Federal Reserve made the mistake of calling Covid era inflation transitory, and now it appears they are set to make the same mistake in reverse on the energy supply shock."

Investors will get even more inflation data on Thursday, with the September reading on producer prices due out at 8:30 a.m. ET. New retail sales figures and weekly jobless claims are also slated for release at that time.

The corporate earnings season continues as well, with regional banks U.S. Bancorp and PNC due to report. Charles Schwab is also scheduled to post earnings.

Asia-Pacific markets were set to fall Thursday, tracking losses on Wall Street ashotter-than-expected U.S. inflation datafuels concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates more aggressively.

Escalating attackson commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have also dented sentiment, as they add to uncertainty around the Middle East conflict, clouding the outlook for energy supplies.

Futures for Hong Kong'sHang Seng indexstood at 24,074, lower than the index's last close of 24,314.17.

Japan'sNikkei 225was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 66,365 and 66,480, respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 67,744.29.

Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was down 0.85% in its first hour of trade.

Rocket Labshares slipped in extended trading after the company pushed back the launch date of its Neutron rocket to 2027.

Shares last traded lower by about 7%.

The company recently identified an issue with the manufacturing process on one of its propellant domes, according toa Rocket Lab videothat shared details on the launch delay.

Considering the length of time it would take to build a new dome, as well as to investigate and resolve the  manufacturing issue, the company pushed Neutron's first launch date into the new year, according to the video.

CoreWeaveshares were lower by 0.6% after the bell following a sharp pullback for the company's stock and bonds on fears some tech companies are borrowing too much for AI.

The neocloud name nosedived 15.5%, while yields on its debt jumped. CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves in a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

Dow Jones Industrial Average futuresrose just 6 points.S&P 500 futuresfell marginally along withNasdaq-100 futures.

title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
content: Figure caption,Watch: The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil is in Arizona to hear from residents about the expansion of data centres.ByKali HaysTechnology reporter, San FranciscoPublished1 hour agoA year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ââNow, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country."This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it."I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernautA new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according toa report by,externalPew Research Center.Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand."This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation."There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago."People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."New national polling,externalshows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.Yet,recent research,externalfrom Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.Image source,Stephanie MaldonadoImage caption,LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, has made stopping data centre development one of their key issuesArizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position.Recent polls,externalhave found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in aprivate memo,externalthat Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres."This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle", the NRSC added.Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".It could play a part in the state's upcoming senate race too.Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".Image source,ReutersImage caption,Democrat James Talarico has made data centres a part of his campaign for SenateMany of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand."There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project."She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"GUIDE: What are the US midterms?IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightropeEXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lostNEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxRelated topicsUnited StatesUS midterm elections 2026Artificial intelligence

title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
content: Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the USBySam FenwickBusiness reporterPublished1 hour agoOn the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words â "Made in China".Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according toUS government figures.,externalLast year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (Â£7.4bn),trade figures show.,externalWith Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.The factoryGuangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to AmericaEvery toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.Image source,MihoxImage caption,The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 peopleSo, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.Image source,MihoxImage caption,Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail priceAverage pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said onereport,externalat the start of this year.Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.The shipFrom the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.The US borderOnce the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China."We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.The US toy companyImage source,Basic FunImage caption,Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the countryThe cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys."It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.Related topicsInternational BusinessWorld of BusinessChinaChina economyTrump tariffsGlobal tradeUS economyChina-US relationsMore on this storyHow oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from CanadaPublished7 days agoThe wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fallPublished2 OctoberHow the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boomPublished24 September

title: Jim Cramer explains why even strong bank earnings couldn't save their stocks
content:
The nation's biggest banks delivered mixed third-quarter results this week, but Wall Street's reaction was overwhelmingly negative, with all six major bank stocks falling despite some strong results.

CNBC'sJim Cramersaid Wednesday, on Day 2 of the financial earnings flood, that investors appear more concerned about what lies ahead than what the banks just reported.

"Frankly, it's strange to see such universally negative reactions to a set of quarters that contained plenty of positives," the "Mad Money" host said. "But this is what happens when investors are worried about the future, and it's hard not to worry with persistent inflation, rising interest rates, and newly wobbly capital markets."

Here's what stood out from each bank's report.

Wells Fargoreported a mixed quarter Tuesday, beating earnings estimates but falling short on revenue. Net interest margin — a key profitability gauge, measuring the spread between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — stabilized at 2.43%, slightly ahead of expectations. That stabilization was particularly encouraging after the bank had missed net interest margin estimates in nine of the previous 10 quarters. Shares fell following the report, but Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio used by the CNBC Investing Club,upgraded the stockto a buy-equivalent rating. "CEO Charlie Scharf emphasized that his bank is set up to do much better in a higher interest rate environment and, given his track record, I believe him," Cramer said. Wells Fargo stock rose slightly Wednesday.

JPMorgan Chasemissed expectations on both the top and bottom lines on Tuesday. Weakness in fixed income trading and asset management weighed on results, while expenses rose faster than revenue. On the earnings call, though, management offered better-than-expected net interest income forecasts for the fourth quarter and 2027. The stock initially struggled but recovered much of its losses as investors digested the outlook. For Cramer, the quarter "wasn't much of a needle-mover for the world's largest bank." JPMorgan stock gained nearly 1% in Wednesday's awful market.

Citigroupdelivered one of the stronger headline reports on Tuesday. Revenue grew 8% year over year, marking the bank's best third-quarter performance in a decade, while management raised its full-year net interest income outlook. Citi also stood out as the only major bank to exceed fixed-income trading revenue expectations. Despite those positives, shares tumbled 5.6% following the report. "My suspicion is that Citi's stock was punished for its recent outperformance," Cramer said. "Before yesterday's beatdown, it was running circles around the rest of the group. But if you believe in the turnaround, as I do, this is a buying opportunity." Citi shares dropped another 1.8% on Wednesday.

On Wednesday,Bank of Americadelivered one of the most disappointing reports of the group, missing revenue and earnings expectations while also contending with a$1.2 billion regulatory penaltytied to alleged violations of anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws. The bank's capital markets businesses were particularly weak, with investment banking fees declining 11% and fixed-income trading revenue falling 17%. Although management highlighted continued growth in deposits and lending, those positives weren't enough to offset the disappointing results. Shares fell roughly 5% following the print.

Goldman Sachs"put up some excellent numbers" Tuesday, comfortably beating top and bottom line estimates. Investment banking fees rose 21%, while equities trading revenue surged 72%, offsetting weaker-than-expected fixed-income trading. Management also struck an optimistic tone, highlighting opportunities to finance the AI infrastructure buildout and a robust investment banking backlog. Yet shares surrendered an early rally and finished Tuesday slightly lower. "When a company reports such strong numbers and the stock gets slammed anyway, that tells you there are a lot of skeptics out there," he said. "They think the boom times are over. I don't agree, but that's the market's verdict, at least for the moment." Cramer's Charitable Trustupgraded Goldman to a buy-equivalentrating following the report, viewing the pullback as a buying opportunity. The stock lost another 1.5% on Wednesday.

Morgan Stanleyalso topped expectations on Wednesday. The bank's Institutional Securities Group, which houses its investment banking and sales and trading segments, saw revenue rise 18%, while wealth management revenue grew 10%. CEO Ted Pick said that he was "cautiously optimistic about the fourth quarter," with the bank reportedly positioned to leadAnthropic'santicipated IPO. Still, shares fell almost 3% despite the solid results, reflecting investors' reluctance to reward even better-than-expected earnings amid broader concerns about the banking sector.

title: Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge
content:
A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields forNvidia-backedCoreWeavecontinued to reach new heights. (Anarticle in The Financial Timesthat the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showingCoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%.Nebius GroupandIren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

title: OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
content:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national charged with secretly installing a recording device in an executive conference room atOpenAI, had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest, federal prosecutors told a judge in a newly unsealedcourt filing.

Alfozan "has the means — and will have the incentive — to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the Oct. 8 filing, which asked a judge to seal a criminal complaint against him and a warrant for his arrest.

The filing said the tickets were booked for Oct. 12, from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul.

The judge granted the sealing request, and Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9, the Department of Justice has said.

He has been detained since his arrest.

Alfozan, 35, is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists a prince from that nation's ruling royal family as a fellow partner.

The VC firm,Raed Ventures, says on its website that Alfozan, who lives in the San Francisco area, "is a seasoned technology professional with deep experience in startups, entrepreneurship, and scaling tech companies."

"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.

Raed, which focuses on investments in the Middle East, announced Alfozan had joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025, two days after Raed said PrinceKhalid Bin Bader Al Saudhad joined as a venture partner. A venture partner usually is a consulting or project-based role, not an investing partner or director who is responsible for raising funds or leading deals.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, according to the Department of Justice. The company said it terminated him this month.

TheFinancial Times reportedWednesday that when Saudi tech influencers visited San Francisco in September, "it was Alfozan who welcomed them to OpenAI offices where he gave them tours."

A former CIA official with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the nature of their past work, told CNBC that Raed Ventures is "basically a state organ" of the Saudi government. One of Raed's funds in December 2024 received an investment fromSaudi Venture Capital, a subsidiary of SME Bank, which is part of Saudi Arabia's National Development Fund.

In addition to being a venture partner in Raed, the prince, Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, is a member of the ruling Al Saud family, and the managing director and vice chairman of his family's private office, according to his bio on Raed's website.

The former CIA official said that if Alfozan's alleged bugging of OpenAI is part of a state-sponsored espionage effort, it shows that "in the AI and tech boom, even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia has assessed that the risk is worth the gain to engage in economic espionage against a close ally."

The former official also said this incident is "probably the tip of the iceberg."

Thecriminal complaintagainst Alfozan does not allege that Raed or its other partners were aware of Alfozan allegedly planting a recording device at OpenAI.

The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, according to the Department of Justice.

Alfozan is charged in U.S. District Court in San Francisco with one count of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.

He is being detained pending an Oct. 19 detention hearing, where his lawyer could argue for his release on bond. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, DOJ said.

Alfozan is not charged with corporate espionage or stealing trade secrets.

OpenAI earlier this yearheld discussions withSaudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the AI company.

Raed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNBC has also requested comment from the Saudi embassy in Washington.

Alfozan's criminal defense attorney, William Pernik, told CNBC by email, "At this point, the information provided has been extremely limited, as the charging documents have just been unsealed yesterday."

OpenAI declined to comment on Wednesday about whether it knew about Alfozan's position at the Saudi firm. And the company said it can't share more details about the conference room in question due to operational security concerns.

The company said in a post onXon Tuesday, "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

"We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,"the company said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."

Alfozan, in a recent interview with the podcastIdentity Capitalabout his career, noted that in July 2016, he and other Saudi nationals who were working at various tech companies in Silicon Valley met with their nation's now-de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The prince was visiting Silicon Valley as part of a U.S. tour to promote his "Vision 2030" economic diversification plan.

"One of the issues we discussed was whether we should move back to [the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia] now and bring our technical skills to improve the economy ... or should we work a few more years before we go back in order to gain more experience," Alfozan said in the interview, which was conducted in Arabic, translated by CNBC and posted online Sept. 24.

Bin Salman replied that "the country was undergoing major development and did not have the talent to train the next generation who would carry on those development plans," Alfozan said.

Alfozan added that the group of young workers "decided it was best to continue to learn and develop our skills before taking our knowledge back to [Saudi Arabia] to improve the tech sector."

Throughout the podcast, Alfozan discusses in detail his trajectory from coding in high school in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to his career in the U.S. At one point in the interview, he refers to himself as an "introvert," who still pushes himself to help other young professionals find success in Silicon Valley.

Days after the podcast was posted, on Sept. 30, a federal criminal complaint alleges that OpenAI staff discovered "a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in" a conference room.

The device, which had a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage, was concealed in toilet paper, according to the complaint.

Alfozan had no authority to enter the conference room, which is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," according to the complaint.

The conference room can be reserved "only by executives and executive assistants," and is typically used "for internal leadership meetings and technical and product sessions, as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts," the complaint said.

Closed-circuit TV footage at OpenAI showed Alfozan close to the conference room on multiple days in September at various times, according to the complaint.

The filing also said that in August, and again in September, Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, as well as "external partner meetings."

And a chatbot associated with Alfozan's spouse, which the complaint alleges shared several identifying characteristics with his own account, allegedly submitted detailed prompts about building, customizing, installing and remotely accessing a recording device. Alfozan's spouse, who was not identified in the complaint, has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

After the recording device was found hidden in the TV in the conference room, OpenAI placed a camera in that room, the complaint says.

Alfozan was seen on that camera entering the conference room at about 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 5, and "checking behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted," the complaint alleges.

That same day, the complaint said, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a printer room at OpenAI.

Inside that bag, OpenAI security found his wallet, ID and "another recording device" made by the same Chinese manufacturer, Seeed, which made the device found inserted in the conference room's TV, the complaint says.

The second recording device, like the first one, "had a recording microcontroller," and "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the complaint said.

Alfozan reported to OpenAI that he had lost the bag, which was returned to him without the second recording device, according to the complaint. He did not inquire about the device, although he asked about certain other items that he said were missing, the complaint said.

title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
content:
Eight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday alleging that theartificial intelligencecompany's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents.

Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have individually sued OpenAI in their own state courts, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said ina release. She said Iowa's lawsuit aims to "vindicate the rights of Iowans affected by OpenAI's willful, dangerous, reckless, and unlawful conduct."

"OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Bird said in a statement. "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend. My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law."

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections into its product that "many other AI products lack." He added that OpenAI is working with states to advance policies that will apply to the entire industry.

"While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,"Pusateri said.

OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children. In a number ofwrongful death lawsuits, ChatGPT is blamed for driving users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also sued OpenAI in June, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users.

OpenAI has taken steps to enhance safety features for parents and children over the last year, and in August it launched a dedicated experience for minors calledChatGPT for Teens. That product includes a range of educational features and age-appropriate safeguards that are intended to reduce exposure to developmentally inappropriate or harmful content.

"Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore," OpenAI said ina releaseat the time. "But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time."

If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact theSuicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

title: Anduril employee tender offer would value the defense tech startup at $90 billion
content:
Defense tech startupAndurilwill give employees a chance to sell stock through a tender offer that would value the company at roughly $90 billion, CNBC has confirmed.

Bloomberg was thefirst to reportthe news, citing sources familiar with the matter. Anduril confirmed the report to CNBC.

Employees participating in the offering can sell shares at $94.80 apiece. The offer, which opened on Oct. 13 and closes Nov. 9, is capped at $1.3 billion, according to the report.

Bloomberg reported that employees in 16 countries are eligible to participate.

Anduril has been a major winner of the growing U.S. defense tech boom andPresident Donald Trump's plans to reindustrialize the U.S. military. In May, the company closed a $5 billion funding round thatdoubled its valuationto $61 billion.

Co-founder and Oculus headset creatorPalmer Luckeyis among a growing group of defense tech leaders taking on advisory roles in Washington as they compete for key Department of Defense contracts.

This month, the company inked aU.S. Navy shipyard contractworth up to $2.9 billion, shortly after Luckey was named a co-director of Project Meridian, which aims to develop and scale military capabilities.SpaceXrocket maker CEOElon Muskalso joined the initiative.

Founded in 2017, Anduril has gained prominence for its drones, augmented reality headsets and AI software it's developing for the U.S. government and allied governments. Last month, the company made headlines after Iran said it had captured one of its underwater vehicles.

title: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about 'enterprise AI timing'
content:
Dellshares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout.

Hewlett-Packard Enterprise,OracleandSuper Microall joined in the downward slide.

In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE andNetApp, "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing."

Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled.

However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerningrevenue figuresout ofOpenAIand more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloudCoreWeaveplunged15%, wiping out its gains for 2026.

The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers.

"There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time."

The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue.

Memory is anotoriously cyclicalbusiness, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT,reported progressover the weekend on a new chip structure.Micronis down 11% for the week, while South Korea'sSK Hynixhas tumbled 13% in U.S. trading andWestern Digitalhas dropped more than 8%.

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
content:
A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.

The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to theMaritime and Port Authority of Singapore.

"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.

Containers were floating in the water after the vessel sank, Pakistani maritime authorities warned in anavigational alert. It is the third commercial ship sunk during the Iran war, according to theInternational Maritime Organization, a United Nations' agency.

A second Singapore-registered container ship, the GFS Giselle, sustained damage to its hull after it was hit by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday. The ship has arrived at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the Singapore maritime authority said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to thestate news agency Tasnim. But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.

Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.

Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait.

More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.

The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and more than a dozen injured, according to the IMO.

Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased.Oil pricesclosed slightly higher Wednesday.

Exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according todata from Kpler.

Shipments from the Middle East, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed.

Daily crude flows are very volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

title: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
content:
CoreWeave'sstock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.

Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 16%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves in a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.

Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said.

"The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back."

Tech investorChamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090,called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on Xlate Tuesday. That promptedTeslaand SpaceX CEOElon Muskto respond, "yikes."

Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of hisdeep diveinto whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk."

CoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained.

"The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said.

"It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running."

He expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November.

CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares ofOracletumbled 9% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%.

The overall tech sectorbrought down the stock market on Wednesdaywith the Nasdaq Composite losing 1.4%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest.

Another neocloud stock,Nebius, dropped 11%.Dellcratered by nearly 12%.

Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to a jump in supply.

Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according toJPMorgan. By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said.

— CNBC's Seema Mody contributed reporting.

title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
content:
The Treasury Department'sOffice of the Comptroller of the Currencyfound some of thelargest banksserving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweepingreportreleased Wednesday.

The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities.

"Banks should make decisions based on financial risk, not the political or social preferences of their employees or executives," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, according to a transcript of his in remarks Wednesday in Lexington, Kentucky.

The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance PresidentDonald Trumphaspressedsince returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and suedmajor banksfor discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally "debanked" after the Jan. 6, 2021,Capitol insurrection, claims banks havedenied.

The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties onBank of Americaover separateanti-money-laundering failures. At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking.

The review coveredJPMorgan Chase, Bank of America,Citibank,Wells Fargo,U.S. Bank,Capital One,PNC Bank,TD BankandBMO Bank, which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trumpexecutive order.

The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination.

Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiaryWePayclosed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence.

JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business.

"We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer," Gould said. "Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria."

Citi declined to comment. The other banks did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Bank Policy Institute, which represents large U.S. and foreign banks, said in a statement that the industry supports "clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management," adding that political or religious beliefs should not affect access to banking services.

The report also found examples cutting the other way politically.

Capital One declined relationships with anabortion-rightsgroup after noting that about 95% of its political contributions went toDemocrats, and with a public education group whose political arm endorsed only Democratic candidates. It also passed on a gun-rights group over concerns that banking it could look like an endorsement.

The practices extended beyond overtly political groups too, the report indicates.

The OCC found restrictions affecting firearms, fossil fuels, private prisons, tobacco andcryptocurrency, and said some banks' appetite for those businesses shifted with the political climate — risking a "whipsaw" effect between administrations.

All nine banks told the OCC they have since revised or consolidated policies aimed at ensuring fair access. But the regulator said none has fully acknowledged past debanking decisions or created a comprehensive program to remediate affected customers.

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
content:
Bank of Americahas hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models includingAnthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO,Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.

In an interview after the bank'sthird-quarter earningsrelease, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel.

"That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC'sLeslie Picker.

"We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.

The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation andregulatory issuesrelated to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday.

The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which wasreleasedto a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.

They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble.

"We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.

Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's sharesslumped as much as 8% Wednesday— sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary.

"Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.

In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts.

Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.
