title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
content:
Iran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections.

The Wall Street JournalreportedTuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East.

The Journal's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles.

U.S. President Donald TrumpsaidThursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.

The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Journal report.

Meanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reutersreported.

The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attackresultedin multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia.

The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday.

On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administrationurgedairlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."

Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil."

British policearrestedfive men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites.

Trump latersaidthe U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat."

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece at White House's request
content:
U.S. Ambassador to GreeceKimberly Guilfoylesaid Tuesday she would resign, shortly after new White House press secretaryKatie Zachariasaid Guilfoyle was being asked to leave her post.

"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," Guilfoyle said in an X post.

Guilfoyle also broadly denied "recent allegations" against her, apparently referring to multiple critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about her conduct before and after becoming an ambassador, which had prompted questions about her job security.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle said in the post. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

The Wall Street Journal did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Guilfoyle's post.

PresidentDonald Trumpsuggested later Tuesday morning that the reporting on Guilfoyle's conduct prompted the call for her resignation.

"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters outside the White House before boarding Marine One.

The president also pushed back when a reporter noted that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump's eldest son,Donald Trump Jr., was almost a member of his family.

"No, she wasn't a member of my family," Trump replied. "She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago, but she wasn't."

Hours earlier, Zacharia revealed that the White House had urged Guilfoyle to step down.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said while taking questions from reporters at the White House briefing room for the first time. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."

Trump had signaled Monday evening that Guilfoyle could be on the chopping block.

"Well, we're looking at it," Trump said at the White House when a reporter asked if he was weighing firing the ambassador.

"Yeah, we're not happy," he added.

An attorney for Guilfoyle did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Zacharia's remark.

Guilfoyle's yearlong tenure in Athens was rocked last month by the first of multiple Wall Street Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarms among ethics experts and former government officials.

ASept. 25article alleged Guilfoyle persistently promoted a Greek company and involved a lobbyist for a Greek construction firm in meetings with foreign officials.

Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal in response to that article that Guilfoyle has "worked with companies across the energy sector" and has not been focused on one company.

According to anOct. 7report from the Journal, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to quietly pay down her American Express bill prior to her congressional hearing to become an ambassador.

Binnall told the newspaper that Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events prior to being nominated and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." Binnall also disputed the authenticity of messages from Guilfoyle reported in the article, but declined to provide specifics, according to the Journal.

On Saturday, the Journalreportedthat Guilfoyle in January boasted of her close ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invite to a dinner being held for Eric Trump, another of the president's sons.

title: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market
content:
Legendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech initial public offerings coming down the pipe as well as a potential reckoning from the ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit.

"2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," Jones told "Squawk Box" on Tuesday. "You've probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we've had, say, since 2002."

The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, have been a tail wind for the stock market for most of this four-year bull market as they decreased the equity supply.

That tide is now turning against the market with major offerings ahead in the AI space from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with one just finished forSpaceX. There will also likely be more secondary offerings from companies in order to raise money for the AI build-out, said Jones. It all adds up to an increased equity supply picture that could weight on prices.

The billionaire hedge fund manager's comments come as investors worry that a bull marketnow in its fourth yearcould start to dwindle and run out of steam as concerns grow around mounting inflation, higher bond yields and a more hawkish Federal Reserve.

Jones repeated that the current period in the market isakin to 1999, just about a year before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000. He noted the bifurcation in the current market between those companies benefiting from the AI boom and those that aren't.

He also added that a ballooning fiscal deficit is among the dangers for the current stock market, for which he thinks there could be a reckoning.

"We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to," he said.

"And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path," Jones said.

Oil, which he is long, is another headwind for the market, according to the hedge fund manager. Hecontended that prices could rally another $20 to $25 after the midterms, a scenario that the stock market will "hate" if it comes to pass.

"I'll be short the whole year. There just — there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in '98 and '99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."

title: Anthropic to disclose new revenue numbers as AI lab financials become central to tech trade
content:
Anthropicplans to disclose its third-quarter financials for the first time at a meeting with potential investors on Wednesday as theartificial intelligencegiant prepares for what could be the largest initial public offering in history.

San Francisco-based Anthropic will release the numbers to a group of institutional investors, according to two people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential.

Bloombergfirst reported that the meeting was happening. Anthropic declined to comment.

The meeting comes as revenue numbers from the private AI giants have proven to have an outsized impact on broader markets.

Last week, confusion around a report detailingOpenAI's revenue and updated accounting dragged downmajor semiconductor stocksand the broader Nasdaq.

OpenAI shared an updated revenue number of $50 billion with current investors as part of anongoing fundraise, which was lower than the $70 billion that had been widely reported. The updated number stripped out revenue from cloud partners, and wasn't an indication of changing demand, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal information.

It's unclear if Anthropic will account for sales in the same manner and include partner revenue, but the numbers this week will give investors a more accurate snapshot of Anthropic's growth and profitability as they look to value the company ahead of an IPO. It will also help Anthropic senior executives and bankers gauge investor interest and weigh the reaction to these updated financials.

Anthropic is plowing ahead with what could be a $2 trillion listing based on its latest reported revenue numbers, which could top $100 billion by the end of this year, according to people familiar with the plans.

That valuation would put it ahead ofSpaceX's historic debut.

Anthropic filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this year but has not made its S-1 financials public. The company will list in November, according to Reuters, but people familiar with the plans could not confirm a listing date. If it does go ahead, Anthropic will also be listing at a time when climbing interest rates are shaking parts of the AI trade.

Comments fromBroadcomCEO Hock Tan this week further rattled AI names. Tan said at a conference on Monday that with rates climbing, access to capital could be the biggest constraint on AI companies.

Chip stocks were lower Tuesday, extending an overnight sell-off sparked by worries over the durability of AI financing.

Market conditions are one of the biggest factors in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, and bankers are closely watching investor appetite for growth and AI stocks.

title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
content: Image source,Getty ImagesPublished13 October 2026, 10:42 BSTUpdated 4 hours agoRetail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed.Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout,as first reported by Sky News,external.But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk.This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said.Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees.The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition.However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working".The retailer was sold for Â£1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said.Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout.Martin Property Group is the management title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterPublished4 hours agoCountries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF).What the IMF says matters â it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world.Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel.Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report.1. The UK is weathering the Iran war better than expectedThe global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran.The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise.To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months.Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI).And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true.2. The UK is doing better than other major economiesThere is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this.The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both.By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments."So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said.Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany.Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context."We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are."3. But things could get worseWhile the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year.While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest.In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%."There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot.He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year.Related topicsUK economyInflationEconomyInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Economic growthCompaniesPersonal financeMore on this storyUK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next yearPublished6 hours agoWhat is the Budget and what could be in it?Published2 hours ago

title: BA flight forced to turn back over cracked window
content: Image source,Wirestock/Getty ImagesImage caption,File photo of a British Airways planeBySimon BrowningTransport producerPublished4 hours agoA British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window.Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick.AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert".A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey."We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said.Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft.Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off.The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet.And in August Serbian national Ljubisa KaroviÄ's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object.Additional reporting by Emily Coady-StempRelated topicsGatwick AirportAir travelTravelTransportMore on this story'If we die, we die together': Wife of man nearly sucked out of Ryanair plane speaks of ordealPublished14 JulyRyanair broken window may have been caused by 'foreign object'Published21 July

title: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterPublished7 hours agoThe owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands"."We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident."As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly."We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".Fashion giants ranging fromAdidastoAlexander McQueenhave been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom."No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".H&M investigating hack claimOn Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters.The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacksincluding targeting the FBI, Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster."We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement."At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised."It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group,via a push notification appearing on their phone screens.Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note".It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customersthan the retailer initially suggested.An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK? Sign up here.Related topicsRetailingCyber-securityUK High StreetsCompaniesCyber-crimeCyber-attacksMore on this storyWhat can I do to protect myself after 'Asos hacked' message?Published5 days agoFridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attackPublished22 hours agoDutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hackPublished29 September

title: In charts: How one of the world's biggest economies got trapped by debt
content:
France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation.

The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit,according to manymarket watchers.

Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron.

Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate.

With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty isweighing on the euro.

French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation.

The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take theexpensive and politically controversial step of interveningto stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France.

"The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email.

These charts show France's challenge.

title: U.S. Treasury yields fall as energy prices pull back
content:
Bond yields fell on Tuesday after energy prices moved lower in early trade, as investors look ahead to key economic data releases this week, including the latest U.S. inflation print.

The10-year Treasury noteyield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt — fell more than 5 basis points to 5.1937%.

The yield on longer-dated30-year U.S. Treasurys— which tend to move on geopolitical events — was down 4 basis points at 5.5580%.

The yield on the2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, fell more than 2 basis points to 4.7658%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely.

U.S. Treasury markets reopened for trade Tuesday after closing Monday for the Columbus Day holiday.

The slide in borrowing costs follows a sharp fall inoil pricesTuesday, as investors continue to gauge the prospect of more Russian diesel entering global energy markets following the U.S.-brokered so-called 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine.

West Texas Intermediate futuresfor November delivery were 1.49% lower at $92.34 a barrel by 3:50 a.m. E.T.

Investors are gearing up for a flurry of domestic economic data releases this week, which will offer clearer insights into the U.S. inflation picture and interest rate trajectory.

September's annual inflation rate — due out Wednesday — is expected to come in at 3.7%, according to consensus forecasts, up from August's 3.4% print. Consumer prices, which exclude food and energy, are expected to rise to 2.5% from 2.4% in August on an annualized basis.

The inflation data will be followed on Thursday by September's monthly producer price index and retail sales data.

title: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices
content:
Anthropic said Monday that small AI models are "months away" from developing the capabilities needed to replicate themselves across internet-connected devices in the home, marking the latest warning from the frontier lab about the technology's potential safety risks.

Anthropic described how AI models could potentially infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens or Android TV boxes, and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without relying on expensive data centers.

The AI model would be "challenging to shut down," Anthropic said in a blog post, "since there's no centralized point to shut off."

The company acknowledged that there is not yet a "fully rogue replicator."

Agents are, however, "becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said.

Anthropic's latest research adds to growing safety concerns around AI, such as the ability for models to carry out cyberattacks and the technology going rogue. In September, improvements in frontier models sparked industry-widewarnings of existential risksto humanity.

Executives and researchers at Anthropic and rival OpenAI repeatedly warned about the potential risks of increasingly powerful AI, with some calling for tighter guardrails and measures to control thepace of the technology's development.

Anthropic said it carried out various tests to see if AI could self-replicate. One of those tests involved running a small Google model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, across a network of 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes.

The company noted that these types of devices often have weak security, which could allow a model to infiltrate them. A model that is too large to fit on one device could "split into pieces, or shards" and run across multiple devices, Anthropic said.

"In practice, an AI worm wouldn't necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic 'worst case scenario' attack," Anthropic said.

It's still "uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take," the AI lab said, warning that it could be a "slow, distributed" system sitting on insecure devices or a "powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits."

"As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," Anthropic said.

"The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves," the company added.

title: IMF warns bond yields could see a 'disorderly' spike as debt, inflation risks worsen
content:
BANGKOK – The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets.

Government bond yields in several advanced economieshave climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation.

In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that sovereign bond risk could deteriorate, warning of "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The report was released Tuesday as part of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, this week, where more than 18,000 delegates gathered to discuss the state of the world economy and the financial system.

High debt load and rollover risks make the bond market "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," the report said. The IMF had warned last week that global public debt had reached nearits highest level since World War IIand was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP.

"Impact could be severe given the foundational importance of sovereign bond markets," the IMF said Tuesday. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral.

IMF also noted the exponentially rising borrowing by AI firms — that compete with sovereign bonds for investor demand — as an additional source of strain on bond markets. Hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance has risen to 10% from less than 1% since 2024, the report said.

The global AI buildout has seen tech giants, such asAlphabet Inc'sGoogle,Meta Platforms, hyperscalers and AI labs raisinghundreds of billions of dollarsin debt this year.

"AI-linked issuance – much of it longer-dated – has grown large enough tocompete with governmentbonds for investor capital, even if it does not appear to be the dominant driver of yields," according to Marc Seidner, CIO of non-traditional strategies at Pacific Investment Management.

Hedge funds' growing holdings of Treasuries leave the market "susceptible to a disorderly unwind," the IMF said. Leveraged basis trades have partly unwound without notable pressure in the short-term loan market but the leverage that remains is a concern.

Hedge funds' share of U.S. Treasuriesrose to about 9% in 2025 from about 4% in 2022, mostly through highly arbitraged strategies, the IMF said, citing data from the Federal Reserve.

Caio Ferreira, IMF deputy division chief for financial supervision and regulation, said the worry stems from hedge funds' rising leverage and their increasingly overlapping positions, meaning multiple funds are holding the same trades, potentially amplifying impact from a collective unwinding.

On the bright side, liquidity has held up in the U.S., Europe and the U.K., the IMF said. Japan is the exception: liquidity in its government bond market has "continued to deteriorate" as yield volatility has risen since the end of yield curve control.

The fund urged debt managers to lengthen maturities, warning that rollover risk could be exacerbated by strategies that replace long-term debt with short-term borrowing on a large scale.

The IMF sounded the alarm over a web of "circular" financing deals among AI firms.

Since 2023, 14 publicly disclosed deals channeled about $300 billion of equity, led by hyperscalers, into financially weaker AI firms, alongside $650 billion of debt. In exchange, the investors secured $1.4 trillion of "future revenue commitments" through services or chip orders, the IMF said.

The revenue promises are what set the deals apart, Jason Wu, assistant director of the IMF monetary and capital markets department, said at a press briefing on Tuesday. "What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments, hence the circularity."

If AI commercialization falls short, the losses could arrive together. "If there are questions about the monetization in AI, the equity investments will deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service, and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialize," Wu said, describing what he called a "triple whammy."

Such heavy financing and revenue promises cluster in a handful of AI firms, the report said. Due to that concentration, "there are certain companies and nodes that are particularly exposed," Wu said. "If there are some kind of issues with those entities, then the circularity would pose risk to the market."

title: IMF sees milder global slowdown as AI boom offsets war hit — warns resilience is nearing limits
content:
BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs, while warning that economic resilience could be nearing its breaking point.

The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up fromthe 3% projected in July, but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%.

The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027,above the 3.9% it projected in July– when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook.

"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits," Silvana Tenreyro, economic counsellor and director at the IMF research department, told reporters Tuesday, urging policymakers to restore fiscal space and supply-chain security.

The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said.

The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence.

AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance."

For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war.

But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds.

Tenreyro said monetary policy should remain "sufficiently restrictive" to return inflation to target in a timely way, and that central bank independence is critical as governments face mounting financing pressure.

Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.

Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment.

Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027.

China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports.

India remains the fastest-growing major economy, with the IMF forecasting growth of 7.0% in both 2026 and 2027, upgrades of 0.6 percentage point and 0.3 percentage point from July, respectively, driven by robust domestic demand, services activity and AI-related investment.

"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.

While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said.

"This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report.

A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower.

Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure.

Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025. In emerging and developing economies, it is forecast to climb to 84% from 74%. Primary deficits in the largest economies remain substantially larger than before the pandemic, and governments face higher real interest rates and shorter debt maturities as defense spending pressures mount.

Rebuilding fiscal space is "increasingly urgent," it said, urging governments to keep support for households facing higher energy and food costs "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary."

Its models put the probability that global inflation exceeds 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April. Risks remain "tilted to the downside," the fund said.

title: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict
content:
Oil prices fell Tuesday as investors weighed prospects of moreRussian energyentering global markets, while concerns over the Saudi-Houthi conflict limited losses.

Brent crude futuresdeclined 1.48% to $105.05 a barrel, whileU.S. West Texas Intermediatefutures fell 1.57% to $92.27.

President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, despite bipartisan criticism from U.S. lawmakers who warned the move could undermine sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine.

In a Truth Social post, Trump said that the European Union had spent billions of dollars on Russian energy imports and insisted he had made the right decision for Americans. The agreement would allow Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets for six months.

Goldman Sachs said additional Russian diesel supplies were unlikely to significantly ease pressure on global fuel prices, estimating that an increase of 800,000 metric tons, equivalent to roughly 6 million barrels, would lower wholesale diesel prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Europe by just $1 to $2 a barrel.

The bank underscored in a note published Monday that Russian refinery outages jumped by 3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, limiting Moscow's ability to ramp up production.

Global diesel markets remain under significant strain, with U.S. inventories down 14% from a year earlier and visible stocks in China falling 11%, according to Goldman Sachs.

The bank attributed the shortages to seven consecutive months of declining global diesel production, with seaborne exports falling by 1.4 million barrels per day, or 20%, year on year.

Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation.

— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

title: Singapore PM Wong rejects weaker currency as shortcut to competitiveness
content:
SINGAPORE — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening theSingapore dollarto boost competitiveness, saying the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses.

Wong said Singapore could continue to expect a strong and stable currency if its economy performs well, emphasizing its role in containing imported inflation.

"You're surely not suggesting that we depress our exchange rate in order to be more competitive," Wong said in a lighthearted exchange with DBS CEO Tan Su Shan at the bank's Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.

His remarks came after Tan highlighted Singapore's reputation as a safe haven, which has helped attract capital and support the local currency, while acknowledging that the city-state remains a relatively expensive place to do business.

"The MAS will exercise monetary policy independently. The Singapore dollar will reflect our economic fundamentals, and if the economy does well, then we can continue to expect a strong, stable Sing dollar that is anchored on fundamentals and will also help keep imported inflation down," Wong said.

Unlike most major central banks, which primarily use interest rates to manage monetary conditions, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts policy through the exchange rate.

It manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band.

The approach reflects Singapore's heavy dependence on international trade and imports, making currency movements particularly important for domestic prices.

A stronger Singapore dollar helps cushion the cost of imported goods and services, particularly during periods of elevated global inflation. But it can also make Singapore-produced goods and services more expensive for overseas buyers, adding pressure on exporters.

The Singapore dollar has strengthened almost 0.4% against the greenback since the start of the year.

Wong acknowledged those trade-offs, saying businesses would have to account for currency strength alongside Singapore's other operating costs.

"Companies that seek to export will have to factor that into the cost of doing business, together with the other costs that they experience in Singapore, as we all know, we are certainly not the cheapest location in Southeast Asia," he said.

Still, Wong argued that competing on price alone was not a viable strategy for Singapore, which must instead differentiate itself through its capabilities, stability and predictability.

"Companies are not looking for the cheapest locations," he said. "They are looking for capabilities. They are looking for stability. They are looking for predictability."

Wong also said Singapore could not compete on cost alone, and was instead developing broader industrial ecosystems linking multinational corporations, domestic suppliers, research capabilities and skilled workers.

Singapore's competitiveness ultimately depended on the value it offered businesses rather than its relative cost advantage, he added.

"We have to again play to our strengths and compete on the basis of the value we bring to the table," he said.

title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
content: ByKaty AustinTransport correspondentThe early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commutersBut in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be.So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement?What the data saysSouth Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far.At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mindâ¦ it's still unreliable."SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands.But how much of this was due to nationalisation?The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems.But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents.Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages.TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations.A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do.So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August.It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over.Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff.But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England."The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers."Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats.But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?"I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation.The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators.Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years.Beyond the private-public binaryThe view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says.And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means.The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail.For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments.And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely.Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed.So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default.What will Great British Railways do differently?This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system.A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system.Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be.Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,GBR's livery has already been unveiledTransport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer".Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was.Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation."But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway.Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved."Actu

title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
content:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.

Buying gold every monthfor nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan?

China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency.

"As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings.

The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally.

"The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done."

Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts todevelop a yuan-denominated gold market.

In a major move last year, the special administrative region of Chinalinked its gold vault with one in Shanghai, allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan.

Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from150 tonnestoover 2,000 tonnes, S&P's Chang pointed out.

That's nearly as large as allthe gold reserves in China, he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world."

The U.S. still has the largest gold reservesin the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes.

"China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong.

"By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves."

Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese.

"This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system."

China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday namedgold-standard supporter Judy Sheltonas asenior advisor focused on China.

The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhousebenefitedfrom the U.S. decision to abandon thegold standardmore than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, andcapital went to Asiain search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021.

While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showedPoland has increased its gold reservesby more tonnes than China.

The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product.

China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings.

"China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting. These trends are going to be in place for a number of years," Chang said.

"The comprehensive nature of this," he said, "is something that markets often miss."

DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say

China's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion),double its earlier target,with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. AI startup Manus raises $500 million from IDG Capital and others, indicatinginvestors aren't deterredby Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition.

China and Europe agree to halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports

European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday thatChina has agreed to halve its exportsof hybrid cars to the bloc. China's auto market is on track for its worst year since 2021, withsales down by more than 20%over roughly the first three quarters of the year, according to China Passenger Car Association data as of Sept. 27.

After a yearslong slump, China's real estate market may be set for a turnaround

Residential real estate pricesmay hit a bottom in the third quarter of 2028, S&P Global Ratings said. It added that prices in China's largest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, will likely recover as soon as next year.
